docs.title: Current platform baseline (October 2026)
docs.text:
Recommended for new projects

Use ROS 2 Jazzy with Gazebo Harmonic on Ubuntu 24.04. Most maintained maritime packages target this pair, for example VRX, Orca5, auv_controllers, ardusub_driver, and the MVP jazzy branches. Use ROS 2 Lyrical with Gazebo Jetty on Ubuntu 26.04 if a dependency needs it (for example POSIM, the ROS 2 version of DAVE). Plan to leave Humble before its end of life in May 2027.

docs.title: Autonomy frameworks
docs.text: An autonomy framework connects sensing, state estimation, planning, control, and mission execution, so that a vehicle can do a task with little or no operator input. This page lists the open frameworks that the maritime community uses, ROS-based and not.

docs.title: Non-ROS autonomy suites
docs.text:
Many fielded marine vehicles run autonomy outside ROS. You will meet these systems in collaborations, and you can bridge them to ROS.

Project What it does ROS Vehicles Activity MOOS-IvP MIT (oceanai) Behavior-based marine autonomy suite (MOOS middleware and the IvP Helm multi-objective behavior arbiter). Not ROS-based, but common on research and naval vehicles. There is no widely maintained public ROS 2 bridge; most teams write a small gateway. Non-ROS USV AUV ActiveOct 2026 DUNE LSTS (University of Porto) Unified Navigation Environment. Onboard software of the LSTS toolchain, which uses the IMC message protocol. Not ROS-based. Non-ROS USV AUV ActiveOct 2026 Goby3 GobySoft Autonomy middleware designed for marine robots on slow and intermittent links (interthread, interprocess, and intervehicle publish-subscribe), with MOOS interoperability. Non-ROS AUV USV ActiveSep 2026 Neptus LSTS (University of Porto) Command, control, and mission review software of the LSTS toolchain (IMC protocol). Non-ROS AUV USV ActiveOct 2026

Bridging to ROS

  • MOOS-IvP: no widely maintained public ROS 2 bridge exists. Most teams write a small gateway node that maps a few MOOS variables to ROS topics.
  • LSTS (DUNE, Neptus, IMC): imc_ros_bridge (ROS 1) lets Neptus command a ROS vehicle.
  • Goby3: designed for slow intervehicle links, with MOOS interoperability. See Communication.

docs.title: Communication
docs.text: A marine robot often has several links with very different bandwidth and latency. Design the software for the worst link the vehicle will use, and make sure the vehicle stays safe when every link fails.

docs.title: Links compared
docs.text:
Link Typical medium Data rate Latency Range Notes Tether Copper or fiber Mb/s to Gb/s Milliseconds Tether length Normal ROS 2 networking works Wi-Fi and RF radios Air Mb/s (Wi-Fi) to kb/s (long-range radio) Milliseconds Line of sight, hundreds of meters to kilometers Only at the surface; DDS discovery can flood slow radios Cellular Air Mb/s Tens of milliseconds Near the coast Coverage varies; plan for gaps Satellite Air From short messages (Iridium SBD, a few hundred bytes per message) to broadband Seconds (SBD) to tens of milliseconds Global Cost per byte matters for SBD Acoustic modem Water Tens of bit/s to tens of kbit/s Seconds (sound travels about 1500 m/s) Hundreds of meters to kilometers Shared, half-duplex, lossy, and affected by the environment Optical modem Water Up to Mb/s Milliseconds Meters to tens of meters, clear water only Needs pointing and clear water

Water absorbs radio waves within centimeters to meters, so sound is the only practical long-range link underwater.

docs.title: ros_acomms
docs.text:
ros_acomms from the WHOI Acoustic Communications Group carries ROS messages over acoustic links and Iridium. It provides:

  • compact encoding of ROS messages into packets, with configurable field codecs (configured per message type, or by introspection)
  • a priority queue manager that decides what to send in each slot
  • media access control (MAC) to share the channel between vehicles
  • modem drivers, with the WHOI Micro-Modem as the main target
  • a link simulator with a ray-tracing channel model, so that you can test without water

The released versions target ROS 1. A merge request on the WHOI GitLab adds ROS 2 (Humble and Jazzy) support; check the documentation for its release status before you plan around it.

Reference: E. Gallimore, T. Schneider, H. Schmidt, "ROS Message Transport over Underwater Acoustic Links with ros_acomms," IEEE/OES AUV Symposium 2022.

docs.title: Designing for acoustic links
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
  participant Top as Topside
  participant Veh as Vehicle (autonomous)
  Note over Veh: Runs its mission without the link
  Veh-->>Top: Status: position, depth, battery, mission state (tens of bytes)
  Top->>Veh: Command: new waypoint or abort
  Note over Top,Veh: Seconds of latency each way. Packets can be lost.
  Veh-->>Top: Acknowledgment
  Note over Veh: If no contact for T seconds: surface or go to a rally point
  1. Make the vehicle autonomous. The link is for monitoring and high-level redirection, not for control loops or teleoperation.
  2. Send only what matters. Status (position, depth, battery, mission state), waypoint updates, and abort commands. Not video, maps, or full-rate sensor data.
  3. Encode compactly. Use fixed-point fields with the resolution you need (for example DCCL), not raw ROS serialization.
  4. Prioritize. Safety commands first, then mission updates, then diagnostics.
  5. Expect loss. Use acknowledgments and retries for commands, and time-stamp commands so the vehicle can ignore stale ones.
  6. Program autonomous failsafes. Time-based and location-based surfacing, and an abort that does not depend on the link.
  7. Test in the real environment. Range and reliability change a lot with depth, temperature profile, sea state, multipath near the surface and seafloor, and noise from shipping and snapping shrimp.
Why acoustic links behave the way they do
  • Low bandwidth: the usable acoustic band is narrow (kilohertz to tens of kilohertz), and absorption grows with frequency. Longer range means lower frequency and lower rate.
  • High latency: sound travels at about 1500 m/s, so 3 km is 2 seconds one way, before any processing.
  • Multipath: reflections from the surface and seafloor arrive late and interfere, worst in shallow water.
  • Refraction: sound speed changes with temperature, salinity, and depth, which bends the paths and can create shadow zones.
  • Doppler: vehicle motion shifts frequencies and needs compensation.
  • Half duplex and shared: one modem talks at a time on a channel, so multi-vehicle systems need a MAC scheme (for example TDMA).

docs.title: Robot-to-shore networking with ROS 2
docs.text:
• Separate the vehicle and shore domains. Run the vehicle on its own ROS_DOMAIN_ID, and limit discovery with ROS_AUTOMATIC_DISCOVERY_RANGE so that robots on the same network do not see each other by accident.
  • Bridge only selected topics over slow or intermittent radio links. Options: rmw_zenoh (ROS 2 middleware on Zenoh, designed for wireless and intermittent links), rosbridge_suite or foxglove_bridge for web tools, or a small custom bridge.
  • Use QoS deliberately. Best effort for telemetry, reliable for commands, and transient local for mission state that a reconnecting operator station needs.
  • MAVLink is a compact alternative for telemetry on autopilot-based vehicles; QGroundControl and mavros speak it.

docs.title: Add or correct a package
docs.text:
All package tables and the catalog come from one file: data/catalog.yml. Add an entry in the right section:

  - name: my_dvl_driver                       # display name
    repo: https://github.com/me/my_dvl_driver # source repository
    url: https://me.github.io/my_dvl_driver   # optional: docs or website
    branch: jazzy                             # optional: branch to check for activity
    category: drivers                         # see `categories` at the top of the file
    ros: [ros2]                               # ros2, ros1, none
    vehicles: [rov, auv]                      # usv, auv, rov, glider, any
    maintainer: My Lab (University of X)
    description: ROS 2 driver for the Example DVL-100, publishing marine_acoustic_msgs/Dvl and TwistWithCovarianceStamped.
    tags: [dvl, example]

Rules for entries:

  • Be factual. Describe what the project does and which versions it supports, with information from its README or documentation. No marketing words.
  • One or two sentences. Longer explanations belong on the topic pages.
  • Do not add activity data. The last-commit date and archived state are written to data/repo_status.yml by a weekly workflow. Never edit that file by hand.

To show a table of entries on a page, put a placeholder comment in the Markdown. The supported forms are listed at the top of hooks/catalog.py: a table for one category, a table of named entries, the explorer, and the summary tiles.

docs.title: Writing guidelines
docs.text:
• Audience: engineers and students who build marine robots with ROS. Explain marine terms the first time, and link to the Glossary.
  • Accuracy first: link to the source of each fact (README, documentation, datasheet, paper). If you are not sure, say so, or leave it out. Do not invent example numbers that look like specifications.
  • Plain, simple language: short sentences, active voice, one instruction per step. Prefer tables for comparisons.
  • Code must be correct: test code examples, and mark placeholder names clearly.
  • Diagrams: use Mermaid code blocks for flows and architectures; they follow the light and dark themes. Use inline SVG with the mrl-svg-* classes for drawings (see the frame diagram in Conventions).
  • Acronyms: add new ones to includes/abbreviations.md, so readers see the definition when they hover.

docs.title: Control and allocation
docs.text:
Marine vehicles are usually controlled in a cascade: guidance makes a desired velocity or pose, a controller turns it into a desired force and moment (a wrench), and thrust allocation distributes the wrench over the actuators.

flowchart TB
  MIS["Mission<br/>waypoints, behaviors"] --> GUID["Guidance<br/>LOS, path following"]
  GUID -->|"desired velocity / heading"| CTRL["Motion controller<br/>PID, sliding mode, MPC"]
  CTRL -->|"wrench τ"| ALLOC["Thrust allocation"]
  ALLOC -->|"thrust per actuator"| MAP["Thrust → command map<br/>(thruster curve)"]
  MAP -->|"PWM, RPM, or CAN"| ESC["ESCs / motor drivers"]
  EST["State estimate<br/>(odometry)"] --> GUID
  EST --> CTRL

Typical ROS 2 messages along the chain: nav_msgs/Path or waypoints → geometry_msgs/Twist → geometry_msgs/Wrench → per-thruster std_msgs/Float64 or a ros2_control command interface.

docs.title: Thrust allocation
docs.text:
Given a desired wrench \( \tau \) (forces and moments in the body frame) and thrust vector \( f \) for \( n \) thrusters, the allocation matrix \( T \) maps thrust to wrench:

\[ \tau = T(\alpha)\, f, \qquad T \in \mathbb{R}^{6 \times n} \]

Column \( i \) of \( T \) is \( [\,d_i ;\; r_i \times d_i\,] \), where \( d_i \) is the unit thrust direction and \( r_i \) the thruster position relative to base_link. For azimuth thrusters, \( T \) also depends on the angles \( \alpha \). Read the positions and directions from the URDF so that the controller and the simulation use the same geometry (thruster_manager does this).

docs.title: Methods
docs.text:
Method Handles thrust limits Azimuth thrusters Cost Use when Pseudo-inverse \( f = T^{+}\tau \) No No (fixed angles) One matrix product Fixed thrusters, and demands stay well inside the limits Weighted pseudo-inverse No, but can favor some thrusters No One matrix product Some thrusters are weaker, less efficient, or noisier Pseudo-inverse + uniform scaling Keeps wrench direction, shrinks magnitude No Cheap Simple vehicles that saturate sometimes Quadratic programming (QP) Yes: hard limits, rate limits, forbidden zones Yes Solver per cycle Real vehicles that saturate, azimuth thrusters, prioritized axes

The pseudo-inverse is valid for non-square \( T \) (more thrusters than controlled axes): it gives the minimum-norm thrust. Its problem is that it ignores limits, not that \( T \) is non-square.

docs.title: Tested example
docs.text:
A vectored layout with four horizontal thrusters, controlling surge, sway, and yaw:

allocation_example.py (output below is real)
import numpy as np

# Thruster x, y (m, FLU body frame) and thrust direction angle (rad, from +x, CCW)
thrusters = np.array([
    [ 0.15,  0.11, np.deg2rad(-45)],   # front left
    [ 0.15, -0.11, np.deg2rad( 45)],   # front right
    [-0.15,  0.11, np.deg2rad(-135)],  # rear left
    [-0.15, -0.11, np.deg2rad( 135)],  # rear right
])
x, y, a = thrusters.T

# Rows: surge force, sway force, yaw moment (z component of r x d)
T = np.vstack([np.cos(a), np.sin(a), x * np.sin(a) - y * np.cos(a)])
T_pinv = np.linalg.pinv(T)

tau = np.array([30.0, 0.0, 3.0])       # 30 N forward, 3 N*m yaw
f = T_pinv @ tau                        # [  6.53  14.69  -6.53 -14.69]

f_max = 10.0                            # thruster limit (N)
f_clip = np.clip(f, -f_max, f_max)      # wrench -> [23.4, 0, 1.28]  direction changes
f_scaled = f * min(1.0, f_max / np.abs(f).max())  # wrench -> [20.4, 0, 2.04]  direction kept

Clipping each thruster on its own changes the ratio between surge and yaw (here from 10:1 to 18:1), so the vehicle turns less than commanded. Scaling keeps the ratio. A QP allocator can do better: for example, it can keep yaw and give up some surge.

docs.title: Known issues
docs.text:
Pseudo-inverse allocators (thruster_manager, thruster allocation matrix controllers)
  • Saturation is not handled. Commands beyond the thruster limits are clipped downstream, which changes the wrench direction (see the example). Use uniform scaling or a QP allocator.
  • Ill-conditioned layouts. If thrusters are nearly parallel, \( T \) is close to singular and small wrench changes give large thrust changes. Check np.linalg.cond(T) at design time.
  • Dead zones. Many thrusters give no thrust below a minimum command. Small demands then do nothing, which can cause limit cycles in station keeping. Compensate in the thrust-to-command map.
QP allocators (mvp_control and others)
  • Solve time varies. Monitor the solve time; reduce the problem size or the control rate if it causes jitter.
  • More parameters. Weights and constraints need tuning. Start with equal weights and add constraints one at a time.
All allocators
  • The thruster curve matters as much as the allocation. Thrust is roughly proportional to RPM squared and is asymmetric forward and reverse. Use the manufacturer's thrust curve at your supply voltage, or measure it on a test stand.
  • Thrust falls with battery voltage. Compensate, or retune when the battery type changes.
  • Thruster interaction. Thrusters close to each other or to the hull lose thrust. Field results are often lower than test-stand results.

docs.title: Station keeping (dynamic positioning)
docs.text:
Holds position and heading for inspection, sampling, or intervention. Common approaches:

  • PID per axis with feed-forward of buoyancy and known currents. Simple and effective for small ROVs. Use anti-windup, because thrusters saturate.
  • Sliding mode control, robust to model uncertainty and common in the marine control literature.
  • Impedance and whole-body control for vehicles with manipulators; auv_controllers includes both, together with twist and trajectory controllers.
  • Model predictive control (MPC) handles constraints explicitly but needs a model and more compute.

docs.title: Path following and guidance
docs.text:
Line-of-sight (LOS) guidance is the classic marine method. For a straight path segment with path angle \( \pi_p \) and cross-track error \( e \), the desired course is

\[ \chi_d = \pi_p - \arctan\!\left(\frac{e}{\Delta}\right) \]

where the lookahead distance \( \Delta \) sets how fast the vehicle converges: a smaller \( \Delta \) converges faster but can oscillate. In a current, add integral action (integral LOS) or estimate the crab angle, because heading and course differ. The sign depends on how you define \( e \); keep it consistent with your frame convention.

Other options: pure pursuit, vector field guidance, and Nav2 controllers on surface vehicles (for example Regulated Pure Pursuit), with the vehicle modeled as differential drive.

docs.title: Underactuated vehicles
docs.text: Torpedo AUVs and most ASVs cannot push sideways. Control surge speed, heading or course, and depth or pitch, and let guidance handle the path. Do not command sway velocity to an underactuated vehicle.

docs.title: Low-level integration
docs.text:
Approach How Good for ros2_control Hardware interface plugin that writes thruster commands; controllers such as auv_controllers run in the controller manager Clean real-time separation, standard tooling Autopilot ArduSub, ArduPilot Rover, or PX4 runs stabilization; ROS sends setpoints through mavros or DDS Fast start on BlueROV2 or BlueBoat, built-in failsafes Direct node A node converts thrust to PWM through a PWM board (for example PCA9685) or a CAN bus Small custom vehicles

Keep a hardware failsafe

Whatever the stack, make sure that the thrusters stop when commands stop: use a command timeout in the driver or ESC, and a kill switch the operator can reach. Software watchdogs are not a substitute for a physical cut-off on a vehicle with exposed propellers.

docs.title: Frames and conventions
docs.text: Frame and sign errors cause more lost days in marine robotics than any algorithm. ROS uses one set of conventions, and marine instruments, textbooks, and autopilots often use another. This page gives the rules, the conversions, and a tested code example.

docs.title: The two conventions
docs.text:
ROS ENU and FLU frames compared with marine NED and FRD frames On the left, the ROS convention: world x east, y north, z up, and body x forward, y left, z up. On the right, the marine convention: world x north, y east, z down, and body x forward, y right, z down. ROS (REP 103) Marine / aerospace World: ENU x East y North z Up Body: FLU x Forward y Left z Up World: NED x North y East z Down Body: FRD x Forward y Right z Down Yaw positive counter-clockwise from East Heading positive clockwise from North Red is x, green is y, blue is z. All four frames are right-handed. ROS convention Marine and aerospace convention Defined by REP 103 SNAME (1950), Fossen, most INS and DVL vendors, ArduPilot and PX4 internally World frame ENU: x east, y north, z up NED: x north, y east, z down Body frame FLU: x forward, y left, z up FRD: x forward, y right, z down Heading / yaw Yaw, counter-clockwise from east Heading, clockwise from north (compass) Vertical z up; altitude positive z down; depth positive

Rule: inside ROS, publish ENU world data and FLU body data. Convert at the edge of your system, in the driver or the bridge, and say so in the package README. Some packages also publish NED and FRD companion frames for interoperability (for example mavros), but the main tree stays ENU and FLU.

docs.title: The frame tree on a vessel (REP 105)
docs.text:
REP 105 defines the mobile platform frames. On a marine vehicle:

flowchart TD
  earth["earth<br/>(ECEF, optional, for multi-vehicle)"] --> map
  map["map<br/>ENU, fixed to a local datum.<br/>Jumps when GNSS or USBL fixes arrive"] --> odom
  odom["odom<br/>ENU, continuous, drifts.<br/>DVL + INS dead reckoning"] --> base["base_link<br/>FLU, vehicle reference point"]
  base --> dvl["dvl_link"]
  base --> imu["imu_link"]
  base --> depth["pressure_link"]
  base --> gnss["gnss_link (antenna)"]
  base --> sonar["sonar_link"]
  base --> cam["camera_link → camera_optical_frame"]
  base --> thr["thruster_N_link"]
  • map → odom comes from the global estimator (for example a second robot_localization instance with GNSS or USBL). It may jump.
  • odom → base_link comes from the local estimator and must be continuous. Underwater, this is DVL, INS, and depth fusion.
  • base_link → sensors are static transforms from the URDF. Measure lever arms carefully: a 10 cm DVL offset combined with a 30°/s yaw rate gives about 5 cm/s of false lateral velocity if you ignore it.
  • Choose one documented reference point for base_link, for example the center of gravity or the hull reference point that the survey offsets use.
  • Camera images use an optical frame (z forward, x right, y down) under the camera link, per REP 103.

docs.title: Converting NED and FRD data to ENU and FLU
Positions and velocities
docs.text: Quantity From NED / FRD To ENU / FLU World position or velocity \( (n, e, d) \) \( (x, y, z) = (e, n, -d) \) Body velocity or acceleration \( (u, v, w) \) forward, right, down \( (u, -v, -w) \) Body angular rate \( (p, q, r) \) \( (p, -q, -r) \)

docs.title: Heading and yaw
docs.text:
\[ \psi_{\text{ENU}} = \frac{\pi}{2} - \psi_{\text{NED}} \]

Wrap the result to \([-\pi, \pi]\). A compass heading of 0° (north) is a ROS yaw of +90°, and a heading of 90° (east) is a yaw of 0°. Also check whether the device reports magnetic or true heading: ROS yaw in an ENU frame is relative to true east, so apply the magnetic declination for your location if needed.

docs.title: Orientation quaternions
docs.text:
For a full attitude, convert the quaternion; do not convert Euler angles one by one. If \( q_{\text{NED}}^{\text{FRD}} \) rotates FRD body vectors into NED:

\[ q_{\text{ENU}}^{\text{FLU}} = q_{\text{ENU}\leftarrow\text{NED}} \otimes q_{\text{NED}}^{\text{FRD}} \otimes q_{\text{FRD}\leftarrow\text{FLU}} \]

where \( q_{\text{ENU}\leftarrow\text{NED}} = (w, x, y, z) = (0, \tfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}, \tfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}, 0) \) is a 180° rotation about the north-east diagonal, and \( q_{\text{FRD}\leftarrow\text{FLU}} = (0, 1, 0, 0) \) is a 180° rotation about x. The result: roll keeps its sign, pitch changes sign, and yaw is 90° minus heading.

ned_to_enu.py (tested)
import math
import numpy as np

# Quaternions are (w, x, y, z).
Q_NED_TO_ENU = np.array([0.0, math.sqrt(0.5), math.sqrt(0.5), 0.0])
Q_FLU_TO_FRD = np.array([0.0, 1.0, 0.0, 0.0])


def qmul(a, b):
    """Hamilton product a * b."""
    w1, x1, y1, z1 = a
    w2, x2, y2, z2 = b
    return np.array([
        w1 * w2 - x1 * x2 - y1 * y2 - z1 * z2,
        w1 * x2 + x1 * w2 + y1 * z2 - z1 * y2,
        w1 * y2 - x1 * z2 + y1 * w2 + z1 * x2,
        w1 * z2 + x1 * y2 - y1 * x2 + z1 * w2,
    ])


def ned_frd_to_enu_flu(q_ned_frd):
    """Convert an attitude quaternion from NED/FRD to ROS ENU/FLU."""
    return qmul(qmul(Q_NED_TO_ENU, q_ned_frd), Q_FLU_TO_FRD)


def ned_to_enu(n, e, d):
    """Convert a world-frame vector from NED to ENU."""
    return e, n, -d

Check your conversion

Point the vehicle north, level. The NED attitude is the identity quaternion, and the ENU yaw must be +90°. Then raise the bow: NED pitch is positive, and ROS pitch must be negative. Test both cases in a unit test of your driver.

docs.title: Depth, pressure, and altitude
docs.text:
• ROS z is up, so z = −depth in the map and odom frames. Keep depth positive only in names and displays (for example a topic called depth).
  • sensor_msgs/FluidPressure is in pascals, not bar or dbar.
  • A simple conversion is \( d = (p - p_{\text{atm}}) / (\rho g) \) with \( g = 9.80665\ \text{m/s}^2 \), \( \rho \approx 1025\ \text{kg/m}^3 \) for seawater and \( \approx 998\ \text{kg/m}^3 \) for fresh water. A 1% error in density gives a 1% error in depth. For survey-grade depth, use the TEOS-10 equations (for example gsw.z_from_p in the GSW Python package), which also account for latitude.
  • Measure \( p_{\text{atm}} \) at the surface before each dive, because weather changes it by several kilopascals (1 kPa is about 10 cm of water).
  • Altitude is the distance to the seafloor (from the DVL or an altimeter). Publish it as sensor_msgs/Range, not as a position.

docs.title: Geographic coordinates
docs.text:
• Publish fixes as WGS 84 latitude, longitude, and ellipsoidal altitude in sensor_msgs/NavSatFix.
  • For a local metric frame, use a local tangent plane (ENU) at a documented datum, or UTM. robot_localization's navsat_transform_node does this for the EKF.
  • At survey scale (more than a few kilometers), a flat-earth approximation adds errors. Use GeographicLib (LocalCartesian) or the geodesy package from geographic_info.
  • UTM grid north differs from true north by the grid convergence angle, up to a few degrees. Account for it when you compare compass heading with a UTM-aligned frame.

docs.title: Units
docs.text: Use SI units, per REP 103: meters, seconds, radians, meters per second, pascals, kilograms. Convert knots, feet, degrees, and decibars in the driver. Note that sensor_msgs/Temperature is in degrees Celsius.

docs.title: Time
docs.text:
Stamp every message with the time of measurement, in ROS time:

  • Synchronize computers with PTP (best) or NTP and chrony. Where a GNSS receiver is present, use its PPS output as the time source.
  • If a device has its own clock, convert its timestamps to ROS time and record the offset. Do not stamp with the time that the serial line delivered the data: DVL and sonar data can arrive tens to hundreds of milliseconds after the ping.
  • In simulation, set use_sim_time: true on every node, including the EKF and your own nodes.
  • Acoustic fixes (USBL, LBL) refer to the time the signal left or arrived, often seconds before the message reaches the vehicle. robot_localization can process delayed measurements if you set smooth_lagged_data: true and a history_length longer than the delay.

docs.title: Networks and QoS
docs.text:
• Use SensorDataQoS (best effort, small queue) for high-rate sensor streams, and reliable QoS for commands and mission state.
  • DDS discovery over Wi-Fi, cellular, or radio links to shore often fails or floods the link. Limit discovery with ROS_AUTOMATIC_DISCOVERY_RANGE and ROS_DOMAIN_ID, or use rmw_zenoh or a bridge for the shore link.
  • Never carry raw DDS over an acoustic link. See Communication.

docs.title: Checklist for a new vehicle
docs.text:
• All world data in ENU and all body data in FLU, with conversions documented per driver
  • Heading converted to yaw, with true or magnetic reference documented
  • Every sensor has a measured, static transform from base_link
  • Depth published as negative z; pressure in pascals
  • All drivers stamp at the time of measurement; clocks synchronized
  • ros2 run tf2_tools view_frames shows one connected tree: map → odom → base_link → sensors
  • Bow-up and north-facing unit tests pass for every attitude source

docs.title: Share your dataset
docs.text:
A useful dataset release has:

  1. Documentation: sensors with models and mounting, calibration, environmental conditions, and how the data was collected.
  2. Standard formats: ROS 2 bags in MCAP for multi-sensor data, plus common image and point cloud formats. Metadata in YAML or JSON.
  3. Ground truth, with a description of how it was obtained and its accuracy.
  4. A clear license (for example CC BY 4.0) and a citation.
  5. Permanent hosting with a DOI (for example Zenodo or an institutional repository).

Then add it to this page with a pull request: name, link, contents, platform, and license.

GNSS sensor_msgs/NavSatFix Fuse it through navsat_transform_node, not directly. USBL / LBL fix geometry_msgs/PoseWithCovarianceStamped or geographic_msgs/GeoPoseStamped No dedicated community message exists yet. Give a realistic covariance. Imaging sonar marine_acoustic_msgs/ProjectedSonarImage or RawSonarImage sonar_image_proc can display and convert these. Multibeam / profiling sonar marine_acoustic_msgs/SonarDetections or SonarRanges Also publish sensor_msgs/PointCloud2 for generic tools. Radar marine_sensor_msgs/RadarSector, RadarEcho CTD, turbidity marine_sensor_msgs/TurbidityNTU; CTD has no standard message yet Use sensor_msgs/Temperature and FluidPressure for parts of a CTD. AIS Messages from marine_ais

See Frames and conventions for frame IDs, units, and sign conventions.

docs.title: WHOI Deep Submergence Lab software
docs.text: The WHOI Deep Submergence Lab (DSL) maintains ROS 1 drivers and tools for deep submergence vehicles in its Bitbucket workspace. This includes drivers for Teledyne RDI DVLs, inertial navigation systems, CTDs, altimeters, and the ds_msgs message set, plus the ds_sim Gazebo plugins. Some repositories need access approval. The software comes from many years of field use on vehicles such as Sentry and Jason, and is a useful reference when you write a ROS 2 driver for the same instruments.

docs.title: Write your own driver
docs.text:
Many marine instruments have no ROS 2 driver. A good driver is small and predictable:

  1. Separate the protocol from ROS. Put parsing in a plain library with unit tests, and keep the ROS node thin. This also lets you reuse the parser in post-processing tools.
  2. Use a reusable transport. transport_drivers gives serial and UDP nodes for ROS 2.
  3. Use standard messages from the table above, and SI units (REP 103).
  4. Timestamp correctly. Stamp each message with the time of measurement, not the time of publication. If the device gives a hardware time, map it to ROS time and document how. See time synchronization.
  5. Convert frames in the driver. Publish ENU and FLU data, and state in the README when the device outputs NED or FRD.
  6. Report health. Publish diagnostic_msgs/DiagnosticArray (for example through diagnostic_updater) with connection state, data rate, and device status flags such as DVL bottom lock.
  7. Make it configurable. Expose port, baud rate, frame ID, and rates as ROS parameters, and supply a launch file and an example configuration.
  8. Release it. Add CI (action-ros-ci or industrial_ci) and release the package to the ROS build farm so others can apt install it. Then add it to the catalog.

docs.title: Tutorial 1: Drive a boat in VRX
docs.text:
Goal: run the Virtual RobotX simulation and drive the WAM-V with thrust commands.

  1. Install ROS 2 Jazzy and Gazebo Harmonic, then build VRX by following the VRX installation tutorial. The default jazzy branch targets this combination.

  2. Launch a world:

    ros2 launch vrx_gz competition.launch.py world:=sydney_regatta

  3. Look around in a second terminal:

    ros2 topic list | grep wamv
ros2 topic info /wamv/thrusters/left/thrust    # std_msgs/msg/Float64

  4. Drive forward, then turn by commanding the two thrusters differently:

    ros2 topic pub -r 10 /wamv/thrusters/left/thrust std_msgs/msg/Float64 "{data: 200.0}" &
ros2 topic pub -r 10 /wamv/thrusters/right/thrust std_msgs/msg/Float64 "{data: 200.0}"

    Stop both commands with Ctrl+C (and kill %1 for the background one). Change one value to make the boat turn.

Next steps: write a Python node that reads the boat's pose and controls heading with a PID loop; then try the VRX tasks (station keeping, wayfinding). The VRX wiki has tutorials for each.

docs.title: Tutorial 2: Thrust allocation by hand
docs.text:
Goal: understand how a multi-thruster vehicle turns a desired force and moment into thruster commands.

Work through the tested allocation example on the Control page. Then:

  1. Change the thruster angles and see how the condition number of \( T \) changes.
  2. Increase the demand until a thruster saturates, and compare clipping with uniform scaling.
  3. Remove one thruster (delete its column) and check which wrenches are still possible. This is how allocation handles a thruster failure.

docs.title: Tutorial 3: Fuse a DVL with robot_localization
docs.text:
Goal: dead-reckon an underwater vehicle from DVL velocity, IMU attitude, and depth.

  1. Get data: use a simulator with a DVL (Gazebo's DopplerVelocityLog system, POSIM, or Stonefish), or a real DVL with its ROS 2 driver (for example waterlinked_dvl).
  2. Check the messages: robot_localization takes DVL velocity as geometry_msgs/TwistWithCovarianceStamped in the DVL frame, with a non-zero covariance. If the driver publishes only marine_acoustic_msgs/Dvl, add a small conversion node.
  3. Check the transforms: base_link → dvl_link, base_link → imu_link, and base_link → pressure_link must exist (from the URDF).
  4. Configure the EKF with the local EKF configuration: DVL as twist0, IMU as imu0, depth as pose0 with only z.
  5. Verify: drive a square in simulation and compare /odometry/local with the simulator's ground truth in PlotJuggler. Then turn off the DVL input and watch the drift grow.

docs.title: Tutorial 4: Turn a USBL fix into a position
docs.text:
Goal: understand the geometry of an ultra-short baseline fix.

A USBL transceiver measures the slant range \( r \) (from travel time and sound speed) and the direction to the vehicle as an azimuth \( \beta \) and a depression angle \( \gamma \) below horizontal, in the transceiver's frame. In an ENU-aligned transceiver frame (azimuth counter-clockwise from east, z up), the vehicle position is

\[ x = r\cos\gamma\cos\beta, \qquad y = r\cos\gamma\sin\beta, \qquad z = -r\sin\gamma \]

A real system must also add the transceiver's own position and attitude (from the ship's GNSS and INS), and correct for the sound speed profile. Vendor USBL systems do all of this and output a georeferenced position; this example shows only the core geometry.

usbl_to_point.py
import math

import rclpy
from geometry_msgs.msg import PointStamped
from rclpy.node import Node


def usbl_to_enu(slant_range, azimuth, depression):
    """Range (m) and angles (rad) in an ENU-aligned transceiver frame -> x, y, z (m)."""
    horizontal = slant_range * math.cos(depression)
    return (horizontal * math.cos(azimuth),
            horizontal * math.sin(azimuth),
            -slant_range * math.sin(depression))


class UsblDemo(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__("usbl_demo")
        self.pub = self.create_publisher(PointStamped, "usbl/position", 10)
        self.timer = self.create_timer(1.0, self.publish_fix)

    def publish_fix(self):
        # Example fix: 120 m slant range, 30 degrees azimuth, 40 degrees below horizontal
        x, y, z = usbl_to_enu(120.0, math.radians(30.0), math.radians(40.0))
        msg = PointStamped()
        msg.header.stamp = self.get_clock().now().to_msg()  # use the ping time on real data
        msg.header.frame_id = "usbl_transceiver"
        msg.point.x, msg.point.y, msg.point.z = x, y, z
        self.pub.publish(msg)


def main():
    rclpy.init()
    rclpy.spin(UsblDemo())


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

For the example numbers, the vehicle is about 79.6 m east, 46.0 m north, and 77.1 m below the transceiver.

Challenges in practice: outliers from multipath, latency between the ping and the arrival of the fix on the vehicle, and covariance that grows with range. See acoustic positioning.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
• World ENU, body FLU, SI units, radians (REP 103). Convert NED and FRD at the driver.

  • Yaw (ENU) \( = \pi/2 - \) heading (NED). Roll keeps its sign, pitch changes sign.
  • \( z = -\)depth. FluidPressure is in pascals.
  • Stamp at the time of measurement, in ROS time.

docs.text: Click a question to open the answer. Cannot find yours? Ask on ROS Discourse.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
I am brand new. Where do I start?

Read Getting started. The fastest hands-on path is: install Ubuntu 24.04 and ROS 2 Jazzy, do the ROS 2 beginner tutorials, then drive a boat in VRX.

Do I need to know programming?

Basic programming helps, and you can learn the rest as you go. Python is enough for most beginner work in ROS 2. C++ is common for drivers and performance-critical code. If you have never programmed, a free introductory Python course is a good first step.

How much math do I need?

To start: algebra and trigonometry (angles and headings). Later: vectors and linear algebra (frames and transforms), and some calculus and control theory (controllers and estimators). Simulators and libraries do the heavy math, so you can learn it when you need it.

Which operating system?

Ubuntu 24.04 for ROS 2 Jazzy, natively if possible. On Windows, use WSL 2 with Ubuntu 24.04. On macOS, use a Linux virtual machine or a remote Linux computer.

How long does it take to learn?

It depends on your background and goals. Many people can drive a simulated vehicle within a week, and write useful nodes within a few months of regular practice.

docs.title: Software
docs.text:
ROS 1 or ROS 2?

ROS 2. ROS 1 Noetic, the last ROS 1 release, reached end of life on May 31, 2025. Some older marine packages are ROS 1 only; use them for reference, or port them. For new projects, use ROS 2 Jazzy (LTS until May 2029) or Lyrical (LTS until May 2031). See the platform baseline.

Which simulator should I use?

For surface vehicles, VRX. For a BlueROV2, Gazebo Harmonic with ArduSub (Orca5 or bluerov2_ignition). For general underwater work with sonar and DVL, POSIM or Stonefish. For realistic images, HoloOcean or OceanSim. See the simulator selection guide.

Is there a standard set of maritime ROS messages?

Use standard ROS messages where they fit, and marine_msgs (marine_acoustic_msgs and marine_sensor_msgs) for DVL, sonar, and radar data. It is released for ROS 2 from Humble to Lyrical. See Message definitions.

My vehicle turns the wrong way or the EKF diverges. Why?

Most often a frame or sign error: NED data published as ENU, compass heading used as ROS yaw, or depth published as positive z. Read Frames and conventions, then the EKF known issues.

docs.title: Physics questions
docs.text:
Why can't I use GPS underwater?

Water absorbs radio signals within centimeters to meters, so satellite signals do not reach a submerged vehicle. Underwater vehicles use dead reckoning (DVL and INS), acoustic positioning (USBL, LBL), and GNSS fixes when they surface. See Localization.

What is the difference between an AUV and an ROV?

An ROV is tethered and piloted from the surface. The tether gives power and high-bandwidth video, so missions last as long as the support ship stays, but the tether limits range and adds drag. An AUV has no tether: it carries batteries and runs its mission autonomously, with only slow acoustic communication while submerged. Hybrid vehicles can do both. See Vehicle types.

Why is underwater communication so slow?

Sound is the only signal that travels far underwater, and the usable acoustic band is narrow. Acoustic modems carry tens of bit/s to tens of kbit/s, with seconds of latency, and suffer from echoes (multipath) and refraction. Vehicles must be autonomous and send only short status messages. See Communication.

docs.title: Hardware and cost
docs.text:
Do I need to buy hardware to start?

No. Learn ROS, control, and estimation in simulation first. VRX, Gazebo, and Stonefish are free.

What is the cheapest way to build something real?

Join a team that shares equipment. If you build alone, start with a small tethered ROV (cheaper and safer to test than an AUV), test in a pool, buy used parts where safe, and 3D-print non-critical parts. Do not save on seals, connectors, or battery safety.

Where do I buy components?

Blue Robotics sells thrusters, housings, and electronics for small vehicles. Professional sensors come from vendors such as Teledyne Marine, Nortek, Water Linked, SBG Systems, and Sonardyne. See Sensors and components, and check the ROS 2 driver status in Drivers before you buy.

I don't live near the ocean. Can I still do this?

Yes. Simulation needs no water, and pools, lakes, and rivers are good test sites. Many teams test locally and travel for sea trials.

docs.title: Education and careers
docs.text:
I'm in high school. Can I take part?

Yes. The MATE ROV Competition has classes for school students, and all the software tools are free. See Events.

What background do people in this field have?

Robotics, mechanical, electrical, and ocean engineering, computer science, physics, and marine science, and many people who taught themselves. Projects and demonstrated skills matter more than the degree title.

Where do people work?

Ocean research institutions (for example WHOI and MBARI), universities, offshore energy and wind companies, survey companies, defense, aquaculture, environmental monitoring, and robotics startups. Roles include robotics and software engineer, controls engineer, field engineer, ROV pilot and technician, and researcher.

    2. Do the first ROS 2 tutorials (topics, nodes, launch).

Which ROS version?

Use ROS 2 Jazzy on Ubuntu 24.04 with Gazebo Harmonic. Most maritime packages and tutorials target this combination in 2026. Do not start new work on ROS 1: its last release (Noetic) reached end of life in May 2025. See the platform baseline.

On Windows, use WSL 2 with Ubuntu 24.04. Gazebo runs in WSL 2 with GPU support on recent Windows versions, but a native Linux install is faster and causes fewer problems. On macOS, use a Linux virtual machine or a remote Linux computer; ROS 2 and Gazebo on macOS have limited support.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: Plain-language definitions of maritime robotics terms, grouped by topic. Tip: on every page of this site, hover over an acronym (for example DVL or USBL) to see what it means.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text: Marine Robotics / Maritime Robotics Building and operating robots that work in, on, or underwater environments. ROS (Robot Operating System) Open-source software framework for building robot applications. Despite the name, it's not an operating system like Windows or Linux - it's a set of tools and libraries that run on top of an OS (usually Linux). Think of it as a toolkit that helps robots' different parts talk to each other. ROS 2 The current generation of ROS with improved real-time behavior and security features. Autonomy / Autonomous The robot can make decisions and operate on its own without constant human control. An autonomous robot can navigate, avoid obstacles, and complete missions independently. Simulation / Simulator Software that creates a virtual environment where you can test robots without needing physical hardware or water. Like a video game for robots - you can make mistakes safely and test ideas quickly.

docs.title: Surface Vehicles
docs.text: ASV (Autonomous Surface Vehicle) A boat or ship that operates on the water's surface without a crew onboard. It makes its own navigation decisions. USV (Uncrewed Surface Vehicle) Similar to ASV - a surface vessel with no people aboard. The terms are often used interchangeably, though USV can include both autonomous and remotely-controlled vessels. WAM-V Wave Adaptive Modular Vessel - a specific type of catamaran (twin-hull boat) platform used in robotics competitions and research.

docs.title: Underwater Vehicles
docs.text: AUV (Autonomous Underwater Vehicle) A robot submarine that operates independently underwater. No cable to the surface - it follows pre-programmed missions or makes its own decisions. ROV (Remotely Operated Vehicle) An underwater robot controlled by a human operator via a tether (cable). The cable provides power and communication. Like flying a drone, but underwater. UUV (Unmanned Underwater Vehicle) General term for any underwater vehicle without people inside - includes both AUVs and ROVs. Glider A special type of AUV that doesn't have a propeller. It uses buoyancy changes to glide through the water in a sawtooth pattern. Energy-efficient for long missions. Torpedo-shaped AUV An AUV with a streamlined, cylindrical hull (like a torpedo). Efficient for long-distance travel in a straight line. Hovering AUV An AUV with multiple thrusters allowing it to move in any direction and hover in place. Good for detailed inspection work.

docs.title: Sensors and Navigation
docs.text: DVL (Doppler Velocity Log) A sonar-based sensor that measures how fast the robot is moving relative to the seafloor or water. Essential for underwater navigation since GPS doesn't work underwater. Uses the Doppler effect (same physics that makes ambulance sirens change pitch as they pass you). IMU (Inertial Measurement Unit) A sensor that measures acceleration and rotation. Helps the robot know which way is up and how it's oriented. Contains accelerometers and gyroscopes. INS (Inertial Navigation System) A more advanced version of an IMU that can calculate position by tracking all movements. Higher accuracy than a basic IMU. GPS / GNSS (Global Navigation Satellite System) Satellite-based positioning system. Important: GPS doesn't work underwater! Only useful when a vehicle surfaces. GNSS is the generic term for all satellite navigation systems (GPS, GLONASS, Galileo, etc.). Depth Sensor / Pressure Sensor Measures water pressure to determine depth underwater. Deeper water = higher pressure. Simple and reliable. CTD (Conductivity, Temperature, Depth) A sensor package that measures three key ocean properties:   - Conductivity: How well water conducts electricity (indicates salinity/saltiness)   - Temperature: Water temperature   - Depth: How deep the robot is Sonar Uses sound waves to "see" underwater (like bat echolocation). Light doesn't travel far in water, but sound does. Different types:   - Imaging Sonar: Creates pictures from sound reflections   - Multibeam Sonar: Maps the seafloor   - Side-scan Sonar: Creates wide-area images of the seabed   - Forward-looking Sonar (FLS): Detects obstacles ahead Hydrophone An underwater microphone. Listens to sounds in the ocean.

docs.title: Control and Motion
docs.text: DOF (Degrees of Freedom) The number of independent ways a body can move. A car moves in 3 DOF on the road (forward, sideways, turning) but can control only 2 of them directly. A marine vehicle moves in 6 DOF; how many it can control depends on its thrusters:   - Surge: Forward/backward   - Sway: Left/right (sideways)   - Heave: Up/down   - Roll: Rotation around front-to-back axis (like a barrel roll)   - Pitch: Rotation around left-to-right axis (nose up/down)   - Yaw: Rotation around vertical axis (turning left/right) Thruster An underwater propeller that pushes the robot. Most marine robots have multiple thrusters to control different directions. Thrust Allocation The math that figures out how much power to send to each thruster to make the robot move in the desired direction. Azimuth Thruster A thruster that can rotate to point in different directions. More flexible than fixed thrusters. Buoyancy The upward force that makes things float. Submarines and AUVs carefully balance their buoyancy to neither sink nor float. Ballast Weight added to a robot to control buoyancy. Some robots can pump water in/out to adjust their ballast.

docs.title: Control Systems
docs.text: PID Controller A common control algorithm (Proportional-Integral-Derivative). Helps the robot smoothly reach a target position or heading. Like cruise control in a car. Waypoint A target position or GPS coordinate the robot should navigate to. A mission might have many waypoints in sequence. Path Planning Algorithm that calculates the route the robot should take from start to finish, avoiding obstacles. Localization Figuring out where the robot is. Underwater this is hard since GPS doesn't work - robots use DVL, IMU, and sometimes acoustic beacons. SLAM (Simultaneous Localization and Mapping) Building a map of an unknown environment while simultaneously figuring out where you are in that map. Challenging but powerful technique. EKF / UKF (Extended/Unscented Kalman Filter) Mathematical techniques for combining data from multiple sensors to get a better estimate of position and velocity. Handles noisy sensor data intelligently.

docs.title: Communication
docs.text: Acoustic Communication / Acoustic Modem Underwater "wireless" communication using sound waves. Much slower than WiFi (much lower data rates) but works underwater where radio doesn't. WHOI Micro-Modem An underwater acoustic modem developed by the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution, widely used on research vehicles. ros_acomms supports it. RF (Radio Frequency) Traditional wireless communication (like WiFi, cellular, radio). Works great in air, but doesn't work underwater - water absorbs radio waves quickly. Tether The cable connecting an ROV to the surface. Provides power and high-bandwidth communication (like an underwater Ethernet cable). Limits how far the ROV can go. Satellite Communication Communication via satellites. Used by surface vehicles or AUVs when they surface. Expensive but works anywhere on Earth. USBL (Ultra-Short Baseline) Acoustic positioning system that uses sound to track an underwater robot's position from a surface ship. Measures range and bearing (direction). LBL (Long Baseline) A network of underwater acoustic beacons deployed on the seafloor. The robot triangulates its position using these beacons. More accurate than USBL but requires setup.

docs.title: Software and Development
docs.text: Gazebo A widely used robotics simulator. Can simulate physics, sensors, and robot movement in a 3D environment. Free and open-source. VRX (Virtual RobotX) A simulated maritime robotics competition based on Gazebo. DAVE (Dave Aquatic Virtual Environment) An underwater vehicle simulation environment built on Gazebo. The ROS 2 version is now called POSIM. RViz A visualization tool for ROS. Shows you what the robot "sees" - sensor data, camera images, point clouds, etc. Helpful for debugging. Topic In ROS, a named channel where messages are published. For example, /camera/image might be the topic where camera images are published. Like a TV channel - anyone can tune in. Node In ROS, a single program or process that does one specific job. A robot might have many nodes working together (one for camera, one for navigation, one for control, etc.). Message In ROS, data sent over a topic. Has a specific format/structure. Like a package being delivered. Launch File A file that starts multiple ROS nodes at once with their configurations. Convenient for starting complex robot systems. MCAP An open log file format for timestamped robot data, and the default storage format of rosbag2. QoS (Quality of Service) ROS 2 topic settings such as reliable or best effort delivery and queue depth. Important on slow or lossy links. Colcon / Catkin Build tools for ROS. Colcon is used in ROS 2, Catkin was used in ROS 1. They compile your code and set up the workspace.

docs.title: Organizations and Institutions
docs.text: WHOI (Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution) A major ocean research institution in Massachusetts, USA, with a long history in marine robotics and ocean engineering. MBARI (Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute) Ocean research institute in California with significant work in marine robotics. ROS-Maritime The ROS Maritime Community Working Group, an open group in the ROS community that maintains this site, shares interfaces, and hosts monthly meetings. See Community.

docs.title: Competition and Standards
docs.text: RobotX An international maritime robotics competition for autonomous surface vehicles. Teams compete in tasks like navigation, object detection, and docking. MBZIRC (Mohamed Bin Zayed International Robotics Challenge) A major robotics competition that includes maritime challenges. SAUVC (Singapore AUV Challenge) Student-focused underwater robotics competition. Held in Singapore. MATE ROV Competition Popular student competition for remotely operated vehicles. Multiple divisions from high school to university.

docs.title: Coordinate Frames
docs.text: NED (North-East-Down) A coordinate system where: - X points North - Y points East - Z points Down (toward Earth's center) - Common in aerospace and marine navigation ENU (East-North-Up) A coordinate system where: - X points East - Y points North - Z points Up (away from Earth) - The ROS standard for world frames (REP 103) Body Frame A coordinate system attached to the robot that moves and rotates with it. In ROS (REP 103) the body frame is FLU: x forward, y left, z up. In marine and aerospace practice it is often FRD: x forward, y right, z down. See Frames and conventions. FLU / FRD Forward-Left-Up and Forward-Right-Down body frames. ROS uses FLU; many marine instruments and autopilots use FRD. Heading The direction the bow points, measured clockwise from north (true or magnetic). Not the same as ROS yaw, which is measured counter-clockwise from east: yaw = 90° − heading. REP 103 / REP 105 ROS Enhancement Proposals that define units and axis conventions (103) and the map, odom, and base_link frames (105).

docs.title: Miscellaneous Terms
docs.text: Open-source Software where the code is freely available for anyone to use, modify, and share. ROS and most tools in this landscape are open source. URDF (Unified Robot Description Format) An XML format for describing a robot's physical structure (links, joints, sensors). Tells ROS what your robot looks like. TF / TF2 (Transform) ROS system for tracking coordinate frames. Keeps track of where different parts of the robot are relative to each other and the world. Workspace In ROS, a directory containing your code and packages. Where you do development. Package In ROS, a collection of related code, configuration files, and documentation organized together. Like an app or library. Repository / Repo A place where code is stored and version-controlled, usually on GitHub or GitLab. CI (Continuous Integration) Automated testing that runs every time code changes. Catches bugs early.

docs.title: Doppler Velocity Log (DVL)
docs.text:
A DVL measures velocity relative to the seafloor (bottom track) or to the water (water track) from the Doppler shift of acoustic beams, and usually also altitude. It is the main dead-reckoning sensor of most AUVs. See Localization.

Vendor Example products ROS 2 driver Water Linked DVL A50, A125 Official (waterlinked_dvl) Nortek Nucleus, DVL500, DVL1000 Official for Nucleus (nucleus_driver) Teledyne RDI Pathfinder, Tasman, Workhorse Community and lab drivers only LinkQuest NavQuest None public found

Choose by:

  1. Bottom-track range at your operating altitude. Lower frequency gives more range; higher frequency gives better accuracy at short range and is smaller.
  2. Minimum altitude, for vehicles that work close to the bottom.
  3. Depth rating, size, and power, for small vehicles.
  4. Accuracy (long-term velocity error as a percentage of speed) from the datasheet.
  5. Interface and driver: Ethernet or serial, and a maintained ROS 2 driver.
  6. Interference: check how pinging is triggered and synchronized with your sonars and modem.

docs.title: Depth and pressure
docs.text: Pressure sensors give depth with good accuracy, and they are simple and reliable. Compare range, accuracy as a percentage of full scale, temperature compensation, and sampling rate. Example: Blue Robotics Bar30 and Bar100 for small vehicles; Paroscientific and Keller for high accuracy. See depth conversion.

docs.title: GNSS
docs.text:
• Standard GNSS for general surface positioning.
  • RTK GNSS for centimeter-level survey positioning, with a base station or correction service (NTRIP).
  • Dual-antenna GNSS for heading without a magnetometer, important for ASVs at low speed.

Drivers: nmea_navsat_driver, ublox_dgnss, ublox, swiftnav-ros2 (see Drivers).

docs.title: Cameras and lights
docs.text:
• Underwater cameras need in-water calibration (see Perception). Low-light sensors and good lighting matter more than resolution.
  • Strobes and LEDs consume much power; place them away from the camera axis to reduce backscatter.
  • Surface vehicles also use thermal cameras and pan-tilt-zoom cameras.

docs.title: Thrusters
docs.text:
Manufacturer Examples Notes Blue Robotics T200, T500 Brushless, flooded-motor design; need a brushless ESC. The T100 is end of life Tecnadyne Various models Professional subsea thrusters VideoRay Thrusters for VideoRay ROVs Vehicle-specific Teledyne SeaBotix BTD150, BTD300 Teledyne ended SeaBotix vehicle production in 2025; check spare availability

Choose by:

  • Thrust curve at your supply voltage, forward and reverse (they differ), and the current draw. You need the curve for allocation (see Control).
  • Depth rating and pressure tolerance.
  • Control interface: PWM through an ESC (simple) or a digital bus with RPM and current feedback (better diagnostics).
  • Spares and service: on intermittent research use, a few low-cost thrusters plus spares can be better than fewer expensive ones; for continuous commercial use, prefer vendor-supported units with service intervals.
Vehicle Typical configuration Torpedo AUV One stern propeller with fins, or a vectored thruster Small ROV (for example BlueROV2) 6 thrusters (heavy configuration: 8) in a vectored layout Work-class ROV Vectored horizontal plus vertical thrusters, with redundancy ASV Twin thrusters (differential), or propeller and rudder; azimuth thrusters on larger vessels

docs.title: Control surfaces and buoyancy
docs.text: Torpedo AUVs and gliders use rudders and elevators. Gliders and some AUVs use buoyancy engines (pumps or pistons) for vertical motion.

docs.title: Power
docs.text:
• Lithium-ion is the norm. Use a battery management system (BMS), and follow transport and storage rules for lithium batteries.
  • Pressure-tolerant battery packs avoid large housings on deep vehicles.
  • Thrust falls as battery voltage drops; plan for it in control and in power budgets.
  • Surface vehicles can add solar panels or fuel generators.

docs.title: Housings, connectors, and tethers
docs.text:
• Housings: acrylic or polycarbonate tubes for shallow vehicles and cameras; aluminum, titanium, or glass for deeper ones. Check the depth rating with margin.
  • Connectors and penetrators: MacArtney (SubConn), Teledyne Impulse, Seacon, and Blue Robotics penetrators. Connectors are a common failure point.
  • Tethers: neutrally buoyant tethers for small ROVs; fiber for high bandwidth over long lengths. Tether drag dominates in a current.

docs.title: Manipulators
docs.text:
Manufacturer Examples Reach Robotics (formerly Blueprint Lab) Reach Alpha, Reach Bravo Schilling Robotics (TechnipFMC) Work-class manipulators Kraft TeleRobotics Hydraulic manipulators

For ROS: MoveIt 2 for planning, and whole-body or impedance control for the vehicle and arm together.

docs.title: Saving money, and where not to
docs.text:
Save on: used instruments from reputable sources, 3D-printed mounts and fairings, simulation before hardware, and testing each sensor alone before integration.

Do not save on: pressure housings and seals, connectors, the INS (it sets your navigation accuracy), battery safety, and an engineering review of critical systems.

docs.title: Integration examples
docs.text:
Reference architectures and launch patterns that recur across marine vehicles. They are starting points: adapt sensor models, frame IDs, ports, rates, and vehicle parameters to your system, and test in simulation first.

Illustrative, not drop-in

Package and executable names for robot_localization, robot_state_publisher, and tf2 are real. Driver package names (your_dvl_driver and similar) are placeholders. Always check parameter names against the documentation of the version you use.

docs.title: Reference architectures
docs.text:
Survey AUV (torpedo)Hovering AUV / ROV (inspection)ASV (survey)

Forward propulsion with control surfaces or a vectored thruster. Flies survey lines at constant altitude or depth.

flowchart LR
  DVL["DVL<br/>bottom-track velocity, altitude"] --> EKF
  INS["INS<br/>attitude, rates"] --> EKF
  DEP["Pressure<br/>depth"] --> EKF
  GNSS["GNSS<br/>surface only"] -.-> NST["navsat_transform"] -.-> EKFG
  EKF["EKF local<br/>odom → base_link"] --> CTRL
  EKFG["EKF global<br/>map → odom"] --> MIS
  MIS["Mission<br/>survey lines"] --> GUID["LOS guidance<br/>course, depth or altitude"]
  GUID --> CTRL["Speed, heading,<br/>depth / pitch control"] --> ACT["Thruster + fins"]
  SSS["Side-scan / MBES"] --> LOG[("rosbag2")]
  • Underactuated: control surge, heading, and depth or pitch; no sway control.
  • GNSS fixes only at the surface; dead reckoning between them. Add USBL or LBL for long dives.
  • Payload sonars usually log raw data for post-processing rather than feeding the autonomy.

Four or more thrusters, 4 to 6 controlled DOF, station keeping near structures.

flowchart LR
  DVL["DVL"] --> EKF
  IMU["INS / AHRS"] --> EKF
  DEP["Pressure"] --> EKF
  USBL["USBL fix<br/>low rate, outliers"] -.-> EKFG["EKF global"]
  EKF["EKF local"] --> CTRL["Pose / velocity<br/>controller (6-DOF)"]
  CTRL -->|"wrench"| ALLOC["Thrust allocation"] --> THR["Thrusters"]
  CAM["Cameras"] --> PER["Perception"]
  FLS["Forward-looking sonar"] --> PER
  PER --> SUP["Mission supervisor"] --> CTRL
  • Fully actuated in the horizontal plane; allocation must handle saturation.
  • Magnetic heading is unreliable close to steel structures; prefer a gyro-based INS or visual or sonar heading aids.
  • Tethered ROVs can run heavy processing topside.

Twin thrusters or rudder and propeller, GNSS-based navigation.

flowchart LR
  GNSS["GNSS (RTK)"] --> NST["navsat_transform"] --> EKF["EKF"]
  IMU["IMU / dual-antenna heading"] --> EKF
  EKF --> NAV["Nav2 or LOS guidance"]
  RAD["Radar · lidar · AIS · camera"] --> COST["Obstacle map / tracker"] --> NAV
  NAV --> CTRL["Speed and heading control"] --> THR["Thrusters / rudder"]
  MBES["Multibeam"] --> LOG[("rosbag2")]
  • Heading at low speed comes from the IMU or a dual-antenna GNSS, not from the GNSS course.
  • Measure antenna and transducer lever arms; survey data depends on them.

docs.title: Launch pattern: sensors and localization
docs.text:
A ROS 2 Python launch file that starts the vehicle description, two drivers, and the local EKF. Use the EKF configuration from Localization.

launch/localization.launch.py
import os

from ament_index_python.packages import get_package_share_directory
from launch import LaunchDescription
from launch.actions import DeclareLaunchArgument
from launch.substitutions import Command, LaunchConfiguration
from launch_ros.actions import Node
from launch_ros.parameter_descriptions import ParameterValue


def generate_launch_description():
    pkg = get_package_share_directory("my_vehicle_bringup")
    use_sim_time = LaunchConfiguration("use_sim_time")

    robot_description = ParameterValue(
        Command(["xacro ", os.path.join(pkg, "urdf", "vehicle.urdf.xacro")]),
        value_type=str,
    )

    return LaunchDescription([
        DeclareLaunchArgument("use_sim_time", default_value="false"),

        # Static transforms base_link -> sensors come from the URDF
        Node(
            package="robot_state_publisher",
            executable="robot_state_publisher",
            parameters=[{"robot_description": robot_description,
                         "use_sim_time": use_sim_time}],
        ),

        # Placeholder driver packages: replace with your real drivers
        Node(
            package="your_dvl_driver",
            executable="dvl_node",
            parameters=[os.path.join(pkg, "config", "dvl.yaml"),
                        {"use_sim_time": use_sim_time}],
            remappings=[("twist", "/dvl/twist")],
        ),
        Node(
            package="your_depth_driver",
            executable="depth_node",
            parameters=[{"frame_id": "pressure_link",
                         "use_sim_time": use_sim_time}],
            remappings=[("pose", "/depth/pose")],
        ),

        # Local EKF: publishes odom -> base_link and /odometry/local
        Node(
            package="robot_localization",
            executable="ekf_node",
            name="ekf_local",
            parameters=[os.path.join(pkg, "config", "ekf_local.yaml"),
                        {"use_sim_time": use_sim_time}],
            remappings=[("odometry/filtered", "/odometry/local")],
        ),
    ])

For thrust allocation, run an allocator that reads the thruster layout from the same URDF, for example ros2 run thruster_manager thruster_manager_node (see the thruster_manager README for its parameters), or the thruster allocation matrix controller from auv_controllers under ros2_control.

docs.title: Control loop rates
docs.text:
Run inner loops faster than the vehicle dynamics, and outer loops slower:

flowchart TB
  A["Mission manager · ~1 Hz"] -->|"waypoint"| B["Guidance · 5-10 Hz"]
  B -->|"desired velocity / heading"| C["Motion control · 10-50 Hz"]
  C -->|"wrench"| D["Thrust allocation · same rate as control"]
  D -->|"thrust per actuator"| E["Thruster driver · same or higher"]

The rates are typical orders of magnitude, not requirements. The EKF should run at least as fast as the controller that uses it.

docs.title: Sensor timing
docs.text:
• Hardware timing (best): distribute PPS from the GNSS receiver, and use PTP on the vehicle network. Sensors that accept a sync input stamp data in a common time base.
  • Software timing: chrony or NTP on all computers. Stamp at the time of measurement when the device reports it.
  • For processing that needs several sensors together (for example camera and sonar), use message_filters with an approximate time policy:
from message_filters import ApproximateTimeSynchronizer, Subscriber
from nav_msgs.msg import Odometry
from rclpy.node import Node
from sensor_msgs.msg import Image


class CameraWithPose(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__("camera_with_pose")
        image_sub = Subscriber(self, Image, "/camera/image_raw")
        odom_sub = Subscriber(self, Odometry, "/odometry/local")
        self.sync = ApproximateTimeSynchronizer([image_sub, odom_sub], queue_size=10, slop=0.05)
        self.sync.registerCallback(self.callback)

    def callback(self, image, odom):
        self.get_logger().info(f"image at {image.header.stamp.sec}, pose x={odom.pose.pose.position.x:.2f}")

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Could not find a connection between 'map' and 'base_link' 
ros2 run tf2_tools view_frames      # writes frames.pdf with the tree
ros2 run tf2_ros tf2_echo map base_link
ros2 topic hz /tf

Usual causes: the global EKF (map → odom) is not running or has no absolute input yet, a static transform is missing, or two nodes publish the same transform.

The EKF output jumps or drifts away

See EKF divergence: check timestamps first, then covariances, then frames.

The vehicle cannot hold position, thrusters always saturate
  • Trim the buoyancy and balance first; a vehicle that needs constant vertical thrust has little margin left.
  • Compare the desired wrench with the achieved wrench (\( T f \)) from the allocator.
  • Check the allocation matrix condition number and the thruster directions in the URDF; a reversed thruster looks like saturation.
  • Reduce commanded speeds, or add thrust.

docs.title: Localization and navigation
docs.text: GNSS signals do not go through water, so an underwater vehicle estimates its position from dead reckoning (DVL and INS), corrects it with occasional acoustic or surface GNSS fixes, and uses a pressure sensor for depth. Surface vehicles have GNSS but must deal with heading, waves, and multipath.

docs.title: Sensor combinations
docs.text: Vehicle Typical sensors Position accuracy driver Survey AUV DVL + INS (often fiber-optic gyro) + depth; GNSS at the surface; USBL or LBL in some missions DVL bottom lock and INS heading quality; drift grows with distance traveled Hovering AUV / ROV DVL + IMU or AHRS + depth; optional USBL; visual odometry close to structures Heading from the magnetometer is unreliable near thrusters and steel Tethered ROV IMU + depth; position from the topside USBL if needed Topside USBL accuracy ASV GNSS (RTK for survey) + IMU; dual-antenna GNSS for heading GNSS quality; heading at low speed Glider Depth, attitude, dead reckoning from the flight model; GNSS at each surfacing Long dead-reckoning intervals and unknown currents
