docs.title: Dead reckoning with a DVL
docs.text:
A Doppler Velocity Log measures velocity from the Doppler shift of acoustic beams (usually four).

  • Bottom track: velocity relative to the seafloor. This is what you want for navigation. It needs the seafloor within range; range depends on the DVL frequency (higher frequency, shorter range, finer resolution).
  • Water track: velocity relative to a layer of water. In a current this is not velocity over ground, so the integrated position drifts by roughly the current speed times the time. Use it only to bridge short gaps, and give it a large covariance.
  • The DVL measures in its own frame. Publish its mounting transform, and remember that a lever arm from base_link adds a velocity term from rotation (see conventions).

docs.title: Acoustic positioning
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  subgraph USBL["USBL (ultra-short baseline)"]
    direction TB
    SHIP1["Ship or ASV with<br/>transceiver array"] -- "range + bearing" --> V1["Vehicle with<br/>transponder"]
  end
  subgraph LBL["LBL (long baseline)"]
    direction TB
    B1["Seafloor beacon 1"] -- range --> V2["Vehicle"]
    B2["Seafloor beacon 2"] -- range --> V2
    B3["Seafloor beacon 3"] -- range --> V2
  end
System How Pros Cons USBL Topside array measures range (travel time) and bearing (phase) to the vehicle One topside unit; easy to deploy Error grows with range; needs the ship's GNSS and attitude; the fix is computed topside and must be sent to the vehicle LBL Vehicle measures ranges to surveyed seafloor beacons Good accuracy over a fixed area Beacons must be deployed, surveyed, and recovered SBL Several transducers on the hull of the support vessel No seafloor work Accuracy limited by the hull baseline Single-beacon range Ranges to one beacon (for example on the modem) while moving Cheap with an acoustic modem Needs motion for observability

Fuse acoustic fixes in the map frame estimator as absolute pose measurements with realistic covariance and outlier rejection. Account for latency: the fix refers to the time of the ping, not the time it reached the vehicle.

docs.title: robot_localization configurations
docs.text:
Use two estimators, per REP 105: a local EKF (odom frame) with continuous inputs, and a global EKF (map frame) that also takes absolute fixes. The configurations below are minimal, working starting points. Topic names are examples.

Local EKF (odom → base_link)Global EKF (map → odom)navsat_transform_node config/ekf_local.yaml
ekf_local:
  ros__parameters:
    frequency: 30.0
    two_d_mode: false
    publish_tf: true
    map_frame: map
    odom_frame: odom
    base_link_frame: base_link
    world_frame: odom

    # DVL: body-frame velocity, geometry_msgs/TwistWithCovarianceStamped
    twist0: /dvl/twist
    twist0_config: [false, false, false,   # x, y, z
                    false, false, false,   # roll, pitch, yaw
                    true,  true,  true,    # vx, vy, vz
                    false, false, false,   # vroll, vpitch, vyaw
                    false, false, false]   # ax, ay, az

    # IMU / INS: orientation and angular rate, sensor_msgs/Imu in ENU / FLU
    imu0: /imu/data
    imu0_config: [false, false, false,
                  true,  true,  true,
                  false, false, false,
                  true,  true,  true,
                  false, false, false]
    imu0_remove_gravitational_acceleration: true

    # Depth: absolute z (negative below the surface),
    # geometry_msgs/PoseWithCovarianceStamped with only z set
    pose0: /depth/pose
    pose0_config: [false, false, true,
                   false, false, false,
                   false, false, false,
                   false, false, false,
                   false, false, false]
config/ekf_global.yaml
ekf_global:
  ros__parameters:
    frequency: 30.0
    two_d_mode: false
    publish_tf: true
    map_frame: map
    odom_frame: odom
    base_link_frame: base_link
    world_frame: map

    twist0: /dvl/twist
    twist0_config: [false, false, false, false, false, false,
                    true,  true,  true,  false, false, false,
                    false, false, false]
    imu0: /imu/data
    imu0_config: [false, false, false, true,  true,  true,
                  false, false, false, true,  true,  true,
                  false, false, false]
    pose0: /depth/pose
    pose0_config: [false, false, true,  false, false, false,
                   false, false, false, false, false, false,
                   false, false, false]

    # GNSS (surface only), converted to the map frame by navsat_transform_node
    odom0: /odometry/gps
    odom0_config: [true,  true,  false, false, false, false,
                   false, false, false, false, false, false,
                   false, false, false]

    # USBL or LBL fix in the map frame, with outlier rejection
    pose1: /usbl/pose
    pose1_config: [true,  true,  false, false, false, false,
                   false, false, false, false, false, false,
                   false, false, false]
    pose1_rejection_threshold: 5.0   # Mahalanobis distance

    smooth_lagged_data: true         # accept fixes that arrive late
    history_length: 10.0             # seconds; longer than the acoustic latency
config/navsat.yaml
navsat_transform:
  ros__parameters:
    frequency: 10.0
    magnetic_declination_radians: 0.0  # set for your site if the IMU yaw is magnetic
    yaw_offset: 0.0                    # pi/2 if the IMU reports 0 when facing north
    zero_altitude: true
    publish_filtered_gps: true
    use_odometry_yaw: false
    wait_for_datum: false
    # Remap: imu -> /imu/data, gps/fix -> /gnss/fix,
    #        odometry/filtered -> /odometry/global, odometry/gps (output)

Things the configurations do not do for you

  • Covariances. The EKF trusts each input according to its covariance. Every driver must publish realistic values; zero covariance makes the filter fail.
  • GNSS underwater. Gate the GNSS input (for example drop fixes when depth is more than about 0.5 m, or when the fix quality is poor), so that stale or multipath fixes do not pull the estimate.
  • Heading reference. If the IMU heading is magnetic, it is unreliable close to thrusters, batteries, and steel. A fiber-optic or ring-laser gyro INS gives true heading by gyrocompassing.

docs.title: Known issues
docs.text:
DVL
  • Bottom lock lost: at high altitude, over soft sediment, on steep slopes, or in aerated water. The estimate then drifts at the rate of the INS alone. Plan missions inside bottom-lock range, and monitor the DVL status flag.
  • Acoustic interference with sonars and modems: corrupted sonar images and modem packet loss. Trigger sensors in turn or choose separated frequencies.
  • Thruster noise and bubbles degrade returns during high thrust. Mount the DVL away from thrusters.
  • Water track in currents: see above. Do not treat it as velocity over ground.
EKF divergence

Root causes, from most to least common:

  1. Timestamps wrong (wall time instead of ROS time, or stamped at the time of reception)
  2. Covariances too small, so the filter is too confident in a bad sensor
  3. Frame errors (NED data published as ENU, missing or wrong transform)
  4. Bad initial state

Debug:

ros2 run tf2_tools view_frames                   # one connected tree?
ros2 topic echo /diagnostics                     # robot_localization warnings
ros2 topic hz /dvl/twist /imu/data               # rates as expected?
ros2 topic echo /dvl/twist --field header.stamp  # stamps close to now?

Fixes: correct the timestamps first, then increase the covariance of the doubtful sensor (less trust), increase process noise, and disable inputs one at a time to find the culprit. Plot innovations in PlotJuggler: they should be zero-mean.

Intermittent absolute fixes (GNSS, USBL)
  • Jumps in the map frame are expected when a fix corrects accumulated drift. Controllers should run on the continuous odom estimate, and only planners should use map.
  • Outliers from multipath, refraction at thermoclines, or biologic noise: use poseN_rejection_threshold, a median pre-filter, or a gate on the reported quality.
  • Shadow zones: refraction at thermoclines can block acoustic paths. The vehicle then navigates on DVL and INS only.
Covariance tuning takes time
  1. Start with the manufacturers' noise figures.
  2. Set process noise high, then lower it.
  3. Tune one sensor at a time against ground truth (a survey line, a GNSS track at the surface, or a tank with motion capture).
  4. Check that innovations are zero-mean and consistent with their covariance.

docs.title: Path planning
docs.text:
• Surface vehicles: Nav2 works with an ASV modeled as a differential-drive or Ackermann-like robot on a 2D costmap. Add obstacles from radar, lidar, AIS, and charts. COLREGs-aware avoidance is not built in.
  • Underwater: most missions are pre-planned survey lines or waypoints. 3D planning near structures can use mesh_navigation or a custom planner. Always plan with margins for navigation drift.

docs.title: Field operations
docs.text:
Practical guidance for deploying marine robots, from community field experience: checklists, power budgets, failure modes, environmental limits, and maintenance. Adapt every list to your vehicle and to the manufacturers' instructions.

flowchart LR
  P["Plan<br/>objectives, permits,<br/>power budget, abort criteria"] --> R["Prepare<br/>day before:<br/>vehicle, spares, briefing"]
  R --> S["Pre-splash<br/>power-up sequence,<br/>function tests"]
  S --> D["Deploy and monitor<br/>launch, mission,<br/>status checks"]
  D --> RC["Recover<br/>locate, secure,<br/>power down"]
  RC --> PO["Post-mission<br/>data backup, rinse,<br/>inspect, lessons"]
  PO -.-> P

Safety First

Marine robotics operations involve expensive equipment, challenging environments, and potential hazards. Always:

  • Have emergency recovery procedures
  • Never deploy alone; ensure adequate staffing
  • Check weather and sea state forecasts
  • Brief all personnel on safety protocols
  • Have communication backup plan

docs.title: Day Before Deployment
docs.text:
Vehicle Preparation: - [ ] Battery fully charged and voltage verified - [ ] All O-rings inspected (no nicks, cuts, or compression set) - [ ] O-rings lubricated with appropriate grease (silicone or Krytox) - [ ] Pressure housing leak tested (vacuum test if possible) - [ ] All sensors functional (bench test in air) - [ ] Software updated and tested in simulation - [ ] Mission plan loaded and verified - [ ] Data storage cleared (ensure sufficient space) - [ ] Backup battery charged (for recovery)

Support Equipment: - [ ] Launch/recovery equipment tested - [ ] Spare parts packed (O-rings, connectors, tools) - [ ] Communication equipment charged - [ ] Shore computer ready with monitoring software - [ ] Emergency contact numbers programmed - [ ] Weather forecast reviewed

Documentation: - [ ] Mission plan documented - [ ] Risk assessment completed - [ ] Permits/permissions verified (if required) - [ ] Insurance current - [ ] Emergency procedures reviewed with team

docs.title: Shortly Before Splash
docs.text:
System Power-Up Sequence:

  1. DVL check (per manufacturer guidance)
  2. Many DVLs must not ping in air for more than a short time, because this can damage the transducers. Check the manual, and keep pinging disabled on deck unless the manufacturer allows it
  3. Allow the transducers to reach water temperature if the manual recommends it

  4. Verify bottom lock after the vehicle is in the water

  5. IMU calibration

  6. Power on IMU
  7. Allow gyro bias stabilization per manufacturer guidance

  8. Verify orientation output makes sense

  9. GPS fix acquisition

  10. Power on GPS
  11. Wait for a reliable fix (cold starts can take longer)

  12. Log initial position as deployment reference

  13. Depth sensor zero-offset

  14. Power on with sensor at surface (in air or just submerged)
  15. Record zero-offset (atmospheric pressure)

  16. Verify the reading aligns with local conditions

  17. Acoustic modem range test

  18. Power on modem
  19. Perform surface range test with base station
  20. Verify bidirectional communication

  21. Test emergency abort command

  22. Thruster function test

  23. Critical: Keep vehicle restrained
  24. Command each thruster individually
  25. Verify all directions (forward/reverse)
  26. Check for abnormal noise or vibration

  27. Verify thrust allocation produces expected combined motion

  28. Camera/lights check

  29. Power on cameras
  30. Verify image quality and focus
  31. Check lights (may need submersion to verify thermal performance)

Final Checks: - [ ] All hatches properly sealed - [ ] No loose cables or items that could snag - [ ] Abort/recovery line attached (if applicable) - [ ] Team briefed on deployment and recovery procedures - [ ] Visual inspection complete (no obvious damage)

docs.title: During Deployment
docs.text:
Launch phase: - Monitor system status in real-time - Verify sensor data immediately after submersion - Abort if any critical sensor failures - Log deployment time and GPS position

Mission phase: - Monitor periodically (acoustic status updates if available) - Log any anomalies or environmental changes - Be ready for emergency recovery - Track estimated mission completion time

Recovery phase: - Be ready at estimated surface time - Have visual line-of-sight before approach - Secure vehicle promptly (don't let it drift) - Power down in reverse order of power-up

docs.title: Post-Deployment
docs.text:
Immediate (post-recovery): - [ ] Download data promptly, before any other work on the vehicle - [ ] Backup data to multiple locations - [ ] Rinse vehicle with fresh water (if salt water deployment) - [ ] Remove batteries and dry compartments - [ ] Inspect all seals and hatches - [ ] Log any damage or issues

Same day: - [ ] Review data quality and mission success - [ ] Document lessons learned - [ ] Note any anomalies or failures - [ ] Update maintenance log - [ ] Charge batteries for next deployment

Within week: - [ ] Full inspection of all O-rings - [ ] Sensor calibration check - [ ] Review and archive mission data - [ ] Update procedures based on lessons learned

docs.title: Calculating Mission Duration
docs.text:
Basic formula: 

Mission Duration = Battery Capacity (Wh) / Average Power Draw (W) × Efficiency Factor

Efficiency factor: Use a conservative factor that accounts for discharge curves, temperature, and aging. Check your battery datasheet.

docs.title: Example Power Budget - Hovering AUV
docs.text:
Note: This is a template structure. Fill with values from your component datasheets and measurements.

Component Power (W) Duty Cycle Avg Power (W) Notes Onboard Computer TBD TBD TBD Datasheet + measured load DVL TBD TBD TBD Datasheet IMU TBD TBD TBD Datasheet Depth Sensor TBD TBD TBD Datasheet Sonar TBD TBD TBD Datasheet Cameras/Lights TBD TBD TBD Datasheet Thrusters TBD TBD TBD Measured under mission profile Acoustic Modem TBD TBD TBD Datasheet Miscellaneous TBD TBD TBD Converters, comms, auxiliaries Total TBD

Margin: Reserve capacity for contingencies and recovery. Document your policy in the mission plan.

docs.title: Power Optimization Strategies
docs.text:
High-power consumers: 1. Thrusters - Often the largest consumer during transit - Minimize aggressive maneuvering - Use efficient paths - Consider buoyancy gliding if applicable

  1. Lights - Necessary for imaging but power-hungry
  2. Only enable when imaging
  3. Use minimum brightness needed

  4. Consider strobes vs continuous

  5. Computers - Always-on baseload

  6. Use efficient processors where feasible
  7. Disable unused cores/features
  8. Optimize software (avoid busy-wait loops)

Low-power mode: - Disable cameras/lights during transit - Reduce sonar ping rate - Lower computer CPU frequency - Can extend mission duration depending on your hardware

docs.title: Sea State Limits
docs.text:
Surface vehicles (ASV/USV):

Define go/no-go criteria based on vehicle design, operator experience, and local marine forecasts. Document limits in your SOPs and update them based on field experience.

Limitations to consider: - GPS accuracy degrades (antenna motion) - Acoustic modem performance drops (surface bubbles) - Solar panels less effective (shadowing from waves) - Hull slamming can damage equipment

UUV deployment: - Launch/recovery most critical phase - Launch/recovery often has stricter limits than submerged operation - Once submerged, UUV largely unaffected by surface conditions - Deep thermoclines caused by storms can affect acoustics

docs.title: Current Limits
docs.text:
Vehicle capability: - Strong currents can prevent waypoint following and increase power consumption - Define abort criteria based on your vehicle's measured performance

Impact: - Increased power consumption (fighting current) - Poor station-keeping - Mission duration reduced - Path deviations increase

Mitigation: - Plan missions with/across current (not against) - Increase speed margins in planning - Use current profiles if available - Have abort criteria (if drift exceeds X meters)

docs.title: Temperature Effects
docs.text:
Battery performance: - Capacity drops in cold conditions - Very cold environments can cause permanent damage - Use manufacturer derating curves when available

Electronics: - Temperature ratings vary by component - Pressure housings can help stabilize temperature - Sensors may need time to stabilize

Acoustic propagation: - Thermoclines bend sound (can create shadow zones) - Warm surface, cold deep = sound bends down - Affects acoustic modem range and USBL accuracy

docs.title: Depth Limitations
docs.text: Design implications: - Verify depth ratings for every pressure-bearing component - Pressure housing cost increases with depth - DVL range and acoustic performance can limit operations

docs.title: DVL Failure
docs.text:
Symptoms: - No bottom lock - Erratic velocity readings - Beam status errors

Immediate actions: 1. Switch to IMU-only dead reckoning (short term) 2. Surface for GPS fix if possible 3. Reduce mission to lower speed (dead reckoning degrades with speed) 4. Abort if position accuracy critical

Prevention: - Pre-mission warm-up - Check beam status before critical maneuvers - Plan missions within bottom-lock range

docs.title: IMU Failure
docs.text:
Symptoms: - Orientation divergence - Attitude solution errors - High residuals in EKF

Immediate actions: 1. If hovering ROV: Surface immediately (no attitude = no control) 2. If torpedo AUV: May continue with degraded performance 3. Check magnetometer (often fails separately from gyros) 4. Attempt recalibration if possible

Prevention: - Pre-flight calibration - Avoid magnetic interference sources - Temperature stabilization time

docs.title: GPS Failure (Surface Vehicle)
docs.text:
Symptoms: - No fix or stale fix - Large position jumps

Immediate actions: 1. Continue with dead reckoning (DVL + IMU if available) 2. Check antenna connection 3. Check for obstructions (debris on antenna) 4. Try rebooting GPS receiver

Recovery: - Most failures are cable/connector issues - Salt buildup can block antenna - Requires return to shore for repair

docs.title: Acoustic Modem Failure
docs.text:
Symptoms: - No responses to commands - Corrupted messages - Complete silence

Immediate actions: 1. Vehicle continues autonomous mission (if programmed) 2. Wait for scheduled surface (can't command abort) 3. Monitor expected surface location for recovery

Prevention: - Always program autonomous abort conditions - Don't rely solely on acoustic for critical commands - Have time-based or location-based automatic surface

docs.title: Thruster Failure
docs.text:
Single thruster: - Thrust allocation can often compensate - Reduced performance but mission may continue - Monitor power draw on remaining thrusters

Multiple thrusters: - Abort mission - Activate emergency surface procedure - Jettison weights if equipped

Common causes: - Seaweed/debris entanglement - Electrical short - Bearing failure (noise, vibration)

docs.title: Leak Detection
docs.text:
Symptoms: - Water in pressure housing - Conductivity sensor alarm - Unexplained power loss

Immediate actions: 1. Emergency surface immediately 2. All thrusters full up 3. Drop weights if equipped 4. Activate recovery beacon

Prevention: - Careful O-ring maintenance - Vacuum test before deployment - Don't over-torque hatches

docs.title: Controller Instability
docs.text:
Symptoms: - Oscillation in position or attitude - Growing amplitude oscillations - Erratic thruster commands

Immediate actions: 1. Switch to backup controller (if available) 2. Reduce controller gains 3. Emergency surface if unsafe

Common causes: - Incorrect tuning for actual vehicle - Sensor noise not filtered - Actuator saturation causing integrator windup

docs.title: EKF Divergence
docs.text:
Symptoms: - Position estimate jumps - High innovation values - Covariance growing unbounded

Immediate actions: 1. Reset EKF if possible 2. Disable faulty sensor input 3. Switch to primary sensor only (e.g., DVL-only navigation)

Prevention: - Proper covariance tuning - Sensor timeout detection - Outlier rejection

docs.title: Mission Data Collection
docs.text:
Essential logging: - All sensor raw data (for post-processing) - State estimates (position, velocity, attitude) - Control commands (thruster outputs) - System status (CPU, power, temperatures) - Timestamps (synchronized across all sensors)

Data rates: - Sensor rates vary widely by hardware and configuration - Estimate storage based on your configured rates and payloads

docs.title: Post-Mission Processing
docs.text:
Quality checks: 1. Sensor health: Any dropouts or errors? 2. Position accuracy: Compare GPS fixes (if available) 3. Control performance: Did vehicle follow commands? 4. Power consumption: Match predictions?

Data products: - Processed navigation (final position estimates) - Georeferenced sensor data (imagery, sonar) - Mission performance metrics - Lessons learned documentation

docs.title: Mission Planning SOP
docs.text:
1. Define mission objectives (survey area, inspection target, etc.)
  2. Plan waypoints with environmental considerations
  3. Calculate power budget and mission duration
  4. Check environmental forecast (sea state, current, temperature)
  5. Identify abort criteria (sensor failures, position error limits, time limits)
  6. Review emergency procedures with team
  7. Obtain required permissions (if applicable)

docs.title: Deployment SOP
docs.text:
1. Pre-deployment checklist (see above)
  2. Team brief (roles, communication protocol, abort signals)
  3. Power-up sequence (sensors first, thrusters armed last)
  4. Function tests (all sensors, thrusters, modem)
  5. Launch (controlled, documented)
  6. Monitor (periodic status checks)

docs.title: Recovery SOP
docs.text:
1. Estimate surface location (last known position + drift)
  2. Visual acquisition (binoculars, spotter)
  3. Secure vehicle (recovery line/hook)
  4. Power down (reverse of power-up sequence)
  5. Immediate post-recovery (data download, rinse, inspect)

docs.title: Lessons Learned (Community Contributed)
docs.text:
Share Your Experience

Have operational experience to share? Add it to this page with a pull request, or post it on ROS Discourse.

From the community:

docs.title: "Always test acoustics first"
docs.text:
Contributor: Field roboticist

"After loading vehicle on boat and transiting to site, first thing we do is acoustic range test before launching vehicle. Saves hours of debugging if modem isn't working. Can't tell you how many times we caught a bad cable or wrong configuration before splashing."

docs.title: "GPS cold start takes longer than you think"
docs.text:
Contributor: ASV operator

"Budget extra time for GPS to get a solid fix after power-on. Don't rush this. A poor GPS fix at start can corrupt navigation."

docs.title: "DVL needs warm-up"
docs.text:
Contributor: Research engineer

"Once the vehicle is in the water, we power the DVL early and wait for readings to stabilize before we start the mission. We never let it ping on deck."

docs.title: "Fresh water rinse saves equipment"
docs.text:
Contributor: Marine technician

"After every salt water deployment: thorough fresh water rinse. We've saved thousands in corrosion damage with this simple step. Pay attention to connectors - they corrode first."

docs.title: "Document everything"
docs.text:
Contributor: Ocean engineer

"Maintain a detailed log book. Date, time, location, sea state, what worked, what didn't. Future you will thank past you when troubleshooting recurring issues."

docs.title: "Spare O-rings are mission-critical"
docs.text:
Contributor: ROV pilot

"Keep a complete set of spare O-rings at deployment site. Murphy's law: you'll nick an O-ring during assembly. Having spares means mission continues; not having them means mission aborted."

docs.title: After Each Deployment
docs.text:
• Fresh water rinse
  • Visual inspection
  • Data download and backup
  • Battery recharge
  • O-ring inspection

docs.title: Weekly (Active Use)
docs.text:
• Thruster bearing check
  • Connector inspection
  • Software updates review
  • Battery health check

docs.title: Monthly
docs.text:
• Full system test
  • O-ring replacement (preventive)
  • Sensor calibration verification
  • Vacuum leak test

docs.title: Annually
docs.text:
• Complete overhaul
  • Pressure housing hydro test
  • All O-rings replaced
  • Battery capacity test
  • Professional calibration of critical sensors (DVL, INS)

For deployment-specific guidance, see vehicle manufacturer's documentation. This page provides general best practices from community experience.

docs.title: Perception and mapping
docs.text: Light is absorbed and scattered in water within meters to tens of meters, depending on turbidity, while sound travels kilometers. Underwater perception therefore combines sonar for range and coverage with cameras for close-range detail. Surface vehicles add radar, lidar, AIS, and cameras.

docs.title: Acoustic or optical?
docs.text: Sonar Camera Range in water Meters to hundreds of meters, depending on frequency Centimeters to tens of meters, depending on turbidity and light Resolution Lower; falls with range High at close range Works in turbid or dark water Yes Poorly; needs artificial light Main artifacts Speckle, multipath, elevation ambiguity (2D imaging sonar), acoustic shadows Color loss with depth, backscatter, refraction at the housing port Typical use Obstacle avoidance, search, SLAM, bathymetry Inspection, close-range mapping, classification, visual odometry

docs.title: Sonar types
docs.text:
Type Output ROS message (marine_msgs) Typical use Single-beam echosounder (for example Ping2) Range to bottom sensor_msgs/Range Altitude, shallow bathymetry Mechanically scanned imaging sonar (MSIS, for example Ping360) One beam that rotates; a full image builds up over seconds RawSonarImage / ProjectedSonarImage Low-cost obstacle detection, SLAM in confined spaces Multibeam imaging / forward-looking sonar (FLS, for example Oculus) A fan image each ping ProjectedSonarImage Real-time obstacle avoidance, inspection, sonar SLAM Multibeam echosounder (MBES) Many range and angle detections across track SonarDetections / SonarRanges Bathymetric mapping Side-scan sonar (SSS) Wide strips of seabed backscatter on each side No standard message yet Search, survey, archaeology Synthetic aperture sonar (SAS) Very high resolution seabed images No standard message Mine countermeasures, high-resolution survey

Elevation ambiguity: a 2D imaging sonar gives range and bearing but not elevation, so objects at different heights in the beam fall on the same pixel. Sonar SLAM and 3D reconstruction methods must handle this explicitly.

docs.title: Underwater vision
docs.text:
• Calibrate in water. A flat port changes the effective focal length and adds distortion, so an in-air calibration is wrong underwater. Calibrate with a target in the water through the same port, or use a dome port centered on the lens.
  • Color and contrast. Red light is absorbed first. Enhancement and color correction help people and some detectors, but check whether they help your downstream algorithm before you add them to the pipeline.
  • Lighting. Strobes or LEDs placed away from the camera axis reduce backscatter.
  • Visual odometry and SLAM (ORB-SLAM3, OpenVINS, SVIn) work in clear water with texture. They fail in turbid water and over featureless sand, so fuse them with DVL and INS rather than relying on them alone.

docs.title: Underwater SLAM
docs.text:
Approach Sensors Examples Sonar pose-graph SLAM Imaging sonar + DVL + IMU sonar-SLAM (BRUCE, iSAM2 backend) Sonar-visual-inertial Camera + IMU + sonar + depth SVIn Visual or visual-inertial Camera (+ IMU) ORB-SLAM3 (used by Orca5), OpenVINS Bathymetric SLAM Multibeam + navigation Research code; often custom

Factor-graph libraries (GTSAM, fuse) are the common backends. DVL and INS dead reckoning gives strong odometry factors between sonar or camera observations.

docs.title: Seafloor mapping
docs.text:
• Bathymetry from multibeam data needs accurate navigation, attitude, sound speed profiles, and lever arms. Process it with MB-System (open source) or a commercial package.
  • Photomosaics and 3D reconstruction from cameras use structure-from-motion tools; navigation from the vehicle gives a good initial pose.
  • Sound speed varies from about 1450 to 1550 m/s with temperature, salinity, and depth. Use a measured profile (from a CTD or sound velocity probe) for multibeam and acoustic positioning; a constant 1500 m/s gives range and refraction errors.

docs.title: Surface vehicle perception
docs.text:
• Radar sees other vessels and the shoreline at long range. Messages: marine_sensor_msgs/RadarSector and RadarEcho.
  • Lidar is good for docking and nearby obstacles, but is affected by spray, rain, and the water surface.
  • AIS gives positions and identities of equipped vessels: see marine_ais. Many small craft do not transmit AIS.
  • Cameras detect buoys, markers, and small craft; datasets such as LaRS and MODS are on the Datasets page.
  • COLREGs: collision avoidance that follows the collision regulations needs vessel tracking and intent estimation. MOOS-IvP includes COLREGs avoidance behaviors.

docs.title: Datasets and simulation for perception
docs.text: Train and test on public datasets, and generate labeled data with image-focused simulators such as HoloOcean, OceanSim, and UNav-Sim (see Simulation).

docs.text: Sea time is expensive and slow, so most marine robotics software is developed and tested in simulation first. This page groups simulators by the engine they use, and helps you choose one.

docs.title: Simulation practice
docs.text:
1. Match the simulator to the question. Use a fast, simple simulator for mission logic and a high-fidelity one for perception. One simulator rarely does both well.
  2. Use the same interfaces as the vehicle. Publish the same topics, frames, and message types in simulation and on hardware, so that only the launch file changes.
  3. Calibrate against real data. Fit added mass, damping, and thruster curves from tank or field tests. Defaults from another vehicle can be wrong by a large factor.
  4. Add realistic sensor errors. DVL dropouts, acoustic outliers, GNSS loss at the surface, and camera turbidity cause most field failures. Clean simulated sensors hide them.
  5. Run simulation in CI. Headless Gazebo or Stonefish runs catch regressions before sea trials. SUAVE and POSIM publish Docker images you can reuse.
  6. Record your configuration. Keep world files, model parameters, and random seeds under version control.

Expect a sim-to-real gap

Controllers tuned in simulation almost always need retuning on hardware. Simulated sonar seldom models multipath and reverberation well, and wave models are simplified. Use simulation to remove software defects, not to prove field performance.

docs.text:
Most ROS 2 marine vehicles use the same layers. The package names are common choices, not requirements.

  ALLOC --> HW
  ALLOC -. "or via MAVLink" .-> AP --> HW

Two integration styles are common:

ROS 2 does the controlAn autopilot does the control

ROS 2 nodes compute control and thrust allocation and send commands straight to the ESCs or motor controllers, often through ros2_control. This gives full control over the algorithms. Blue with auv_controllers and MVP work this way.

An autopilot (ArduSub, ArduPilot Rover, or PX4) runs the low-level control and the failsafes. ROS 2 sends setpoints through mavros or the autopilot's DDS interface. This is the quick way to automate a BlueROV2 or a BlueBoat. Orca4 and Orca5 work this way.

docs.title: Logging
docs.text:
• Record everything raw. Raw sensor data lets you reprocess navigation and perception after the mission. Record the state estimate and the controller commands too.
  • Use MCAP. It is the default rosbag2 storage format in current ROS 2 releases, and many tools (Lichtblick, Foxglove, PlotJuggler, the mcap CLI) read it.
  • Split and compress. Use --max-bag-duration or --max-bag-size so that a power loss destroys at most one file. The MCAP storage presets (zstd_fast, zstd_small, fastwrite) set the compression.
  • Do not log through slow links. Record on the vehicle and download after recovery.
# Record everything to MCAP with fast zstd chunk compression, in 5-minute files
ros2 bag record -a -s mcap --storage-preset-profile zstd_fast \
  --max-bag-duration 300 -o dive_$(date +%Y%m%d_%H%M)
  • Analyze without ROS. rosbags reads and writes ROS 1 and ROS 2 bags in pure Python, so data scientists do not need a ROS installation.

docs.title: Development environment
docs.text:
• Containers. Docker images make simulation and dependencies reproducible across a team. SUAVE and POSIM publish images; Blue and auv_controllers include development container setups. For GPU simulators, install the NVIDIA Container Toolkit.
  • Workspaces. Use vcs (vcstool) with a .repos file to pin the repositories of a vehicle stack, and rosdep for system dependencies.
  • Target hardware. Many vehicles run on ARM computers (Raspberry Pi, NVIDIA Jetson). Build and test on ARM in CI, or cross-compile, before you go to the field.

docs.title: Continuous integration
docs.text:
• Build and test each package on every pull request with action-ros-ci or industrial_ci.
  • Add a headless simulation test: launch the vehicle in Gazebo or Stonefish, run a short mission, and check that it reaches the waypoints.
  • Add unit tests for frame conversions and message parsing in drivers; these find the expensive bugs early.
  • Release packages to the ROS build farm, so users can install them with apt.

docs.title: Field laptop checklist
docs.text:
• Offline copies of documentation, maps, and charts
  • All dependencies installed; no internet needed to build
  • Same software versions as the vehicle (container image tag or .repos pins)
  • Bag analysis tools installed (PlotJuggler, Lichtblick, rosbags)
  • Enough disk space and a second drive for backups

docs.title: Vehicle types
docs.text:
Maritime robots differ mainly in where they operate (on or below the surface), how they get power and communication (tether or not), and how they move (propellers, thrusters, buoyancy, or sail). Each choice changes the software.

  • Surface vehicles (ASV / USV)

    Work on the surface: survey, monitoring, logistics, and relay for underwater vehicles. GNSS, radio, and solar power are available. Usually 2 or 3 controlled DOF (surge and yaw, sometimes sway).

    Software focus: GNSS and heading fusion, obstacle detection (radar, lidar, AIS, cameras), COLREGs, waves.

  • Torpedo AUVs

    Untethered, streamlined, efficient for long survey lines. Usually underactuated: one propeller plus fins or a vectored thruster.

    Software focus: DVL and INS dead reckoning, depth and altitude control, mission autonomy, acoustic communication.

  • Hovering AUVs and ROVs

    Many thrusters for 4 to 6 controlled DOF; hold station for inspection and intervention. ROVs are tethered and piloted; hovering AUVs are free.

    Software focus: thrust allocation, station keeping, perception near structures, manipulation, teleoperation.

  • Underwater gliders

    Change buoyancy to move in a sawtooth pattern with wings, with no propeller. Slow, but missions last weeks to months.

    Software focus: energy-aware planning, sparse communication at each surfacing, dead reckoning with unknown currents.

docs.title: Specialized platforms
docs.text:
• Autonomous sailboats use wind for propulsion and need sail and rudder control with wind-aware routing. See the rs750 simulation in Simulation.
  • Intervention vehicles carry one or two manipulators for valve turning, sampling, or tool use. Software: MoveIt 2 for arm planning, whole-body or impedance control (auv_controllers), and vehicle station keeping.
  • Hybrid ROV / AUV (HROV) vehicles switch between tethered piloting and free autonomous operation.
  • Wave-powered and energy-harvesting platforms convert wave motion into propulsion or electrical power; see MBARI WEC in Simulation.
  • Bio-inspired vehicles use fins, flippers, or pulsed jets; mostly research platforms.
